title: THEY PROMISED YOU A FINANCIAL BREAKTHROUGH… BUT WHEN WAS THE LAST TIME THEY TOLD YOU TO REPENT?
paragraphs: THEY PROMISED YOU A FINANCIAL BREAKTHROUGH… BUT WHEN WAS THE LAST TIME THEY TOLD YOU TO REPENT?

When the pulpit promises prosperity more often than it preaches repentance, we must ask a terrifying question: Are we leading people to Jesus Christ—or teaching them to chase His blessings while ignoring His Lordship?
Imagine sitting in church with your last few pesos in your pocket.

Your electricity bill is overdue. Your children need food. Your rent is coming due. You've prayed until your voice has gone quiet. You've cried where nobody could hear you. And somewhere between another sleepless night and another morning of pretending you're okay, you begin wondering whether God has forgotten your address.
Then the preacher steps onto the platform.
The music swells.
The congregation rises.
And suddenly, the message sounds like the answer to everything you've been suffering.
“Your financial breakthrough is coming!”
“Your season of lack is over!”
“God is about to release supernatural wealth into your hands!”
People shout. Some cry. Others lift their hands, believing this is finally the moment their lives will change.
Then comes the invitation.
“Sow a seed of faith. Give sacrificially. Show God you're ready for your miracle.”
And there you are.
Holding money you cannot afford to lose.
Wondering whether keeping it means you lack faith.
Wondering whether your children's next meal is standing between you and God's blessing.
Wondering whether heaven is waiting for you to prove your devotion with an offering.
But somewhere beneath the music, the excitement, and the promises, a question begins stirring in your soul.
When did the Gospel become more about getting money from God than being reconciled to God?
And an even more uncomfortable question follows.
Why do some preachers talk more about financial breakthrough than repentance?
Please don't rush past this.
Because the answer is not merely about what happens behind a pulpit.
It is also about what happens inside the human heart.
And if we're willing to be honest, this conversation may expose something in all of us.
Not just the preacher.
Not just the ministry.
Not just the person collecting the offering.
Us.
Because sometimes the message we most desperately want to hear is not the message we most desperately need.
Jesus knew that.
And He loved people enough to tell them the truth anyway.
There is something deeply human about wanting relief.

Nobody should be ashamed of praying for enough money to feed their family. There is nothing sinful about asking God for employment, provision, debt relief, or an opportunity to rebuild after devastating financial loss.
Jesus Himself taught His disciples to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11, KJV).
Not imaginary bread.
Not merely symbolic bread.
Daily bread.
The ordinary necessities of human life matter to our heavenly Father.
The Bible does not command believers to celebrate hunger, romanticize poverty, or pretend financial suffering is painless.
God sees the widow counting her coins.
He sees the father who cannot sleep because his children need school supplies.
He sees the mother trying to stretch one meal into three.
He sees the worker who has done everything responsibly and still cannot get ahead.
Financial hardship is real. And so is God's compassion.
But compassion becomes something else entirely when someone's desperation is used to make promises God never made.
That is where we must become discerning.
Because there is a difference between preaching that God provides and declaring that God has guaranteed everyone listening a financial windfall.
There is a difference between teaching biblical generosity and implying that an offering purchases divine intervention.
There is a difference between encouraging faith and making struggling people afraid that God will withhold His goodness unless they give money.
And there is a difference between a preacher who genuinely wants to help people trust God through financial hardship and one who repeatedly uses their hardship to generate revenue.
We cannot see every preacher's heart.
We should not pretend that we can.
But Jesus did teach us to examine fruit.
And Scripture gives us more than enough light to test the message.
Consider the very beginning of Jesus' public preaching.
Mark 1:15 records His announcement:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
The Greek text contains the words:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
Metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō.
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
The verb metanoeite comes from metanoeō, commonly translated “repent.” It involves a change of mind and direction, a turning that Scripture connects with leaving sin and returning to God.
The verb pisteuete calls people to believe, to place their trust in the good news.
Notice what Jesus announced.
He did not begin by guaranteeing that every person following Him would become wealthy.
He announced the arrival of God's kingdom.
He called sinners to repent.
He called people to believe.
And He offered something greater than temporary relief.
Reconciliation with the living God.
This matters because repentance is not an embarrassing side issue that modern Christianity needs to soften.
Repentance belongs to the very heart of the Gospel's call.
Yet repentance must never be separated from grace.
Jesus was not telling people to make themselves perfect so that God might finally love them.
He was calling them to turn from sin and trust the good news of what God was doing through Him.
Repentance is not a payment for salvation.
It is the fitting response of a heart turning toward the Savior.
And the Savior is not merely offering us a better financial situation.
He is rescuing us from sin and death.

That is why a church can have beautiful music, excellent lighting, overflowing attendance, impressive fundraising, and countless testimonies about money—and still need to ask whether the crucified and risen Christ remains central to its preaching.
A congregation may be financially successful without being spiritually healthy.
A ministry may be growing without growing in holiness.
And a message may make thousands of people feel hopeful without faithfully explaining why Jesus died.
Think about that.
A sermon can make you excited about tomorrow while leaving you unprepared to face eternity.
That is not a small concern.
It is a matter of souls.
And perhaps one reason financial-breakthrough preaching becomes so dominant is that it speaks directly to something people already want.
Relief.
Security.
Comfort.
A way out.
When someone is drowning financially, the promise of immediate prosperity can feel irresistible.
Repentance, however, confronts us.
It asks whether we have made money our master.
Whether we have excused dishonesty.
Whether we have neglected the poor.
Whether we have refused forgiveness.
Whether pride, lust, bitterness, greed, or secret sin has found a comfortable home inside us.
It asks whether we want Jesus Himself—or merely the life we imagine He can give us.
And that is uncomfortable.
But discomfort is not always cruelty.
Sometimes the most loving thing anyone can do is tell us the truth we have been avoiding.
Imagine a doctor who discovers a dangerous illness but decides not to mention it because the patient prefers encouraging conversations.
Instead, the doctor promises renewed energy, improved confidence, and a wonderful future.
The patient leaves smiling.
But the disease remains untreated.
Would we call that compassion?
Of course not.
Yet something similar can happen spiritually when preaching repeatedly celebrates blessings while avoiding sin, judgment, repentance, the cross, and the resurrection.
The congregation leaves feeling inspired.
But people may never hear clearly why they need a Savior.
And this is where the warning becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us have become more concerned about whether God will change our circumstances than whether He is changing our hearts.
We ask Him to open doors.
But resist Him when He tells us to close the door to sin.
We ask Him to increase our income.
But refuse to surrender our greed.
We ask Him to remove our enemies.
But ignore His command to love them.
We ask for restoration.
But refuse to repent of the very behavior destroying our relationships.
We want a breakthrough.
But we do not always want to be broken of our pride.
And if that exposes something in you, please understand: the purpose is not to drive you into despair.
It is to bring you back to Jesus.
Because conviction that leads us toward Christ is not the same as condemnation that tells us to hide from Him.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's goodness leads us toward repentance.
His mercy is not permission to remain unchanged.
His mercy is an invitation to come home.
But why would some preachers avoid emphasizing this?
Sometimes it may be fear.
Fear of offending people.
Fear of declining attendance.
Fear of losing financial support.
Fear that sermons about repentance, holiness, and self-denial will not generate the same enthusiasm as promises of wealth.
Sometimes it may be theological confusion.
A preacher may sincerely believe that material prosperity is the ordinary measure of divine favor, even though the broader witness of Scripture does not support that conclusion.
Sometimes it may be an unhealthy ministry culture where fundraising has become so central that biblical teaching is continually shaped around financial appeals.
And sometimes, tragically, greed may be involved.
Scripture does not leave us without warnings.
In 1 Timothy 6:5, Paul speaks of people who suppose “that gain is godliness.”
The Greek phrase behind that warning is:
πορισμὸν εἶναι τὴν εὐσέβειαν
Porismon einai tēn eusebeian.
In context, the idea is that godliness is being treated as a means of material gain.
Paul immediately contrasts that distorted thinking with the declaration:
“But godliness with contentment is great gain” (1 Timothy 6:6, KJV).
Do you see the reversal?
Some people treat devotion to God as a strategy for becoming rich.
Paul teaches that true spiritual gain is found in godliness joined with contentment.
He continues by reminding believers that we brought nothing into this world and can carry nothing out of it.
Then comes the warning in 1 Timothy 6:9:
“But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.”
Notice that Paul does not say every wealthy person is evil.
He warns about the consuming desire to become rich.
And verse 10 identifies the love of money—not money itself—as a root of all kinds of evil.
This distinction is essential.
Money can feed the hungry.
Money can provide medical care.
Money can fund biblical education, support families, publish Christian books, and make discipleship resources accessible to people who cannot afford them.
Money is a tool.
But money becomes spiritually dangerous when it occupies the place that belongs to God.
And when the pulpit begins to revolve around wealth, the congregation may slowly learn to evaluate Christianity through the wrong lens.
A new car becomes evidence of exceptional faith.
A promotion becomes proof of God's approval.
A large bank account becomes a testimony of spiritual superiority.
And the believer still struggling to pay rent begins wondering whether something is wrong with their relationship with God.
That is a terrible burden to place on a wounded conscience.
Especially when Scripture tells a different story.
Consider the apostle Paul.
He loved Christ.
He preached the Gospel.
He endured suffering for the sake of the Church.
Yet in Philippians 4:12 he wrote:
“I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound.”
He knew what it meant to have plenty.
And he knew what it meant to have little.
Then, in the following verse, he declared:
“I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me” (Philippians 4:13, KJV).
How often have we heard that verse presented as though it guarantees extraordinary financial success?
Yet its immediate context concerns learning contentment through changing circumstances.
Paul's confidence was not that he would always escape hardship.
His confidence was that Christ would strengthen him through hardship.
That is an entirely different kind of breakthrough.
A breakthrough that can happen even when the bills are still unpaid.
A breakthrough that allows someone to remain faithful when the promotion never comes.
A breakthrough that teaches a suffering believer to say, “Lord, I still trust You.”
Not because life is easy.
But because Jesus is worthy.
And consider the Christians described in Hebrews 11.
Some experienced extraordinary deliverance.
Others endured mockery, imprisonment, suffering, and death.
The chapter honors their faith without claiming that every faithful person received material comfort in this life.
Faithfulness cannot be measured simply by financial outcomes.
If wealth were the reliable proof of God's approval, how would we explain the apostles who suffered?
How would we explain faithful believers persecuted for Christ?
How would we explain Jesus Himself?
In Matthew 8:20, Jesus said:
“The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.”
The Son of God did not need a luxurious lifestyle to demonstrate the Father's favor.
His glory was not measured by possessions.
His mission was not to build an earthly empire of comfort.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He came to give His life as a ransom for many.
And when the hour of His suffering arrived, He did not purchase His way out.
He went to the cross.
For us.
That is the Gospel.
Not that Jesus became poor so every Christian would necessarily become financially rich.
But that the eternal Son of God humbled Himself, gave Himself for sinners, and secured riches of grace that money cannot buy.
Second Corinthians 8:9 speaks of Christ, who, though rich, became poor for our sake so that through His poverty we might become rich.
In context, Paul is encouraging generous giving by pointing to Christ's self-giving grace. The verse should not be turned into a universal guarantee of personal wealth.
The riches of redemption cannot be reduced to cash.
Forgiveness is richer than gold.
Reconciliation with God is greater than promotion.
Eternal life is more precious than property.
And a clean conscience before God is worth more than the applause of an entire congregation.
Now consider another scene.
A man comes to Jesus.
He is wealthy.
He is morally serious.
He wants eternal life.
We often call him the rich young ruler.
In Mark 10, Jesus confronts the attachment that holds this man captive.
He tells him to sell what he possesses, give to the poor, and follow Him.
But before we rush to the man's reaction, notice something extraordinary.
Mark 10:21 says:
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him.”
The Greek text includes:
ἠγάπησεν αὐτόν
Ēgapēsen auton.
“He loved him.”
Jesus loved the man.
And because Jesus loved him, He confronted the very thing standing between him and wholehearted discipleship.
The man went away grieving because he had great possessions.
This passage is not a blanket command requiring every Christian to sell everything.
It is a piercing revelation of what happens when possessions become more important to us than obedience to Christ.
And perhaps that is what some modern preaching struggles to confront.
It is easier to tell people that God wants to increase their wealth than to ask whether wealth has become their idol.
It is easier to celebrate a financial harvest than to teach contentment.
It is easier to promise that the next season will be prosperous than to explain that following Jesus may involve sacrifice.
But the love of Jesus is too great to flatter us into spiritual ruin.
He loved the rich man enough to expose his bondage.
And He loves us enough to expose ours.
Still, there is another side of this conversation that we must not ignore.
Some believers have been so wounded by financial manipulation that they now distrust every request for ministry support.
That reaction is understandable.
But Scripture does not teach that all financial support for ministry is wrong.
Jesus and His disciples received practical support for their ministry (Luke 8:1–3).
Paul taught that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14).
Believers in the early Church shared generously so that needs could be met.
Giving is biblical.
Supporting faithful Gospel work is biblical.
Helping ministries publish sound teaching, feed the hungry, care for vulnerable people, and reach others with the message of Jesus is biblical.
But the manner and motive of giving matter.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
The Greek word translated “necessity” is:
ἀνάγκης
Anankēs.
In this context, it refers to compulsion or pressure.
Paul's instruction directly challenges the idea that Christians must be pressured, frightened, or emotionally cornered into giving.
A faithful ministry can explain its needs.
It can invite partnership.
It can ask people to support its mission.
But it should never pretend that money buys salvation, forgiveness, divine protection, or a guaranteed miracle.

Biblically, tithing and voluntary support for a Christian publication or discipleship ministry are not identical categories. Christians differ on how Old Testament tithing commands apply under the new covenant, but giving in the Church is consistently associated with generosity, stewardship, and willing hearts.
For a person who intentionally sets aside part of their regular giving for Gospel outreach, it may be part of their personal stewardship.
But it must remain voluntary.
It must never be portrayed as a payment required to glorify God, earn His favor, or secure a financial breakthrough.
Because the moment we tell people that God's acceptance depends on purchasing access to our ministry, we have contradicted the very grace we claim to proclaim.
And Gospel Warrior must be held to that same standard.
We cannot criticize financial manipulation in other ministries while quietly practicing it ourselves.
That would undermine everything this message stands for.
Instead, our invitation must be rooted in something far more beautiful.
A shared mission.
A love for Scripture.
A desire to see wounded people encounter the real Jesus.
A commitment to reach those who are spiritually exhausted, biblically confused, ashamed of their past, or struggling to find their way back to God.
Because behind every screen is a human being.
Someone may be reading this while sitting beside a hospital bed.
Someone may be reading it after another argument about money.
Someone may be a pastor who has begun measuring success more by offerings than transformed lives.
Someone may have left church because they felt valued only when they could give.
Someone may be a struggling Christian who once believed that financial hardship meant God was disappointed in them.
And someone may have spent years chasing blessings without ever truly surrendering to the Blesser.
If that person is you, listen carefully.
Jesus has not forgotten you.
Your financial situation does not determine your worth.
Your bank balance does not measure your salvation.
Your inability to give to a ministry does not make you less loved by God.
And the cross of Jesus Christ is not an unfinished transaction waiting for your financial contribution.
When Jesus cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30), He was declaring the completion of His redemptive work—not the beginning of a fundraising arrangement.
The Greek word recorded there is:
τετέλεσται
Tetelestai.
“It is finished,” or “It has been accomplished.”
In John's account, this declaration comes at the culmination of Jesus' suffering and His obedient mission.
We must not reduce this sacred moment to a slogan about financial debts.
Its significance is infinitely greater.
Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He gave His life.
He bore our sins.
He opened the way for reconciliation with God.
And through His resurrection, He defeated death.
That is why we do not preach repentance without grace.
And we do not preach grace without Christ.
We proclaim Jesus crucified and risen.
We proclaim forgiveness through Him.
We proclaim the call to repent and believe.
And we proclaim the transforming work of the Holy Spirit in those who belong to Him.
Perhaps the most dangerous thing about a distorted prosperity message is not simply that it can leave people financially disappointed.
It can leave them with a distorted picture of God.
When someone is promised that a specific offering will produce a financial miracle, and the miracle does not happen, they may begin to believe that God has failed them.
They may blame themselves.
They may conclude their faith was too weak.
They may give even more in desperation.
Or they may walk away from Christianity altogether.
Not because the Gospel failed.
But because what they were sold was never the Gospel in the first place.
That possibility should make every Christian communicator tremble.
Including us.
We are dealing with souls, not sales figures.
With human suffering, not marketing opportunities.
With the eternal Word of God, not motivational slogans that can be adjusted to maximize donations.
And yet the answer is not to stop speaking about God's provision.
The answer is to speak about it truthfully.
Tell people to pray for daily bread.
Teach them to work diligently when they are able.
Encourage wise stewardship.
Promote generosity.
Support the poor.
Confront exploitation and dishonesty.
Celebrate God's kindness when He provides.
And remind believers that financial success is neither a guarantee of holiness nor a substitute for it.
But above all, preach Christ.
Preach the Savior who forgave the woman caught in adultery and told her to leave her life of sin.
Preach the Savior who welcomed Zacchaeus, whose repentance was reflected in restitution and generosity.
Preach the Savior who restored Peter after his denial.
Preach the Savior who promised paradise to a dying criminal who had no opportunity to build wealth, establish a ministry, or make a financial offering.
That criminal had nothing impressive to bring.
No prosperity testimony.
No donation receipt.
No years of religious achievement.
He simply turned to Jesus.
And Jesus answered him with mercy.
What a stunning picture of grace.
A man at the end of his life, unable to repair his past, found hope in the crucified King beside him.
That is the kind of Gospel that can reach the person who feels too ashamed to return to church.
That is the kind of Gospel that can reach the woman who believes her mistakes have disqualified her forever.
That is the kind of Gospel that can reach the man who lost everything and thinks he has nothing left to offer God.
Because the central message of Christianity is not that good people can purchase better circumstances.
It is that guilty sinners can receive forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
And that grace changes everything.
This is why the theme of Gospel Warrior is not merely a memorable phrase.
Consider what that means.
The scandal of our sin.
The scandal of religious hypocrisy.
The scandal of greed dressed in spiritual language.
The scandal of wounded believers who have been taught to associate God's love with financial performance.
And then, against that darkness, the astonishing grace of Jesus Christ.
Grace that calls us out of deception.
Grace that invites us to repent.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that restores.
Grace that transforms.
Grace that teaches us to stop using God as a means to an end and begin worshiping Him as our greatest treasure.
But that grace is never a license to exploit people.
It is the very reason we must refuse to do so.
If you are a preacher reading this, please hear the challenge with the seriousness and love with which it is intended.
Your congregation does not merely need another prediction about increased income.
They need the whole counsel of God.
They need to understand sin.
They need to understand the cross.
They need to understand repentance, faith, holiness, forgiveness, suffering, generosity, and eternal hope.
They need biblical teaching that prepares them not only for seasons of abundance but also for seasons of loss.
They need to know how to follow Jesus when their prayers are answered differently than they expected.
And they need to see that the preacher standing before them loves their souls more than their contributions.
If you have drifted from that calling, it is not too late to repent.
You do not have to defend every sermon you have ever preached.
You do not have to preserve an image of infallibility.
You can return to Scripture.
You can correct misleading teaching.
You can become more transparent about finances.
You can restore trust through humility and accountability.
And you can make Jesus Christ central again.
That would be a breakthrough worth celebrating.
If you are a believer who has been hurt by financial manipulation, you do not have to pretend the experience was harmless.
Spiritual wounds can run deep.
But please do not confuse the failures of human messengers with the character of Jesus.
He does not need to deceive you to gain your devotion.
He does not need to frighten you into generosity.
He does not need to promise you luxury to prove His love.
Look at the cross.
There is His love.
Look at the empty tomb.
There is your hope.
Look at His Word.
There is the truth by which every preacher—including this writer—must be tested.
And if you are someone who has been pursuing financial breakthrough while avoiding repentance, this may be your moment to come home.
Not tomorrow.
Not after another sermon.
Not after another promise.
Now.
You can tell Jesus the truth.

“Lord, I have wanted Your gifts more than Your presence. I have asked You to change my circumstances while resisting Your work in my heart. Forgive me. Teach me to trust You. Teach me to follow You, whether I have much or little.”
There is no magic formula in those words.
Salvation is not found in repeating a particular prayer.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ, received through faith in Him.
But an honest cry to God can be the beginning of a life no longer governed by appearances.
And perhaps someone reading this has been carrying a question they have never dared to say aloud.
“Does God still love me if I never become financially successful?”
Yes.
For those who are in Christ, His saving love is not measured by material prosperity.
Romans 8:38–39 reminds believers that neither death nor life, nor any other created thing, can separate them from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Your poverty cannot purchase His love.
Your wealth cannot purchase His love.
Your offerings cannot purchase His love.
And your failures do not place you beyond the reach of His mercy when you turn to Him.
Jesus is not for sale.
Grace is not an auction.
And eternal life is not a reward for the highest bidder.
Now, there is something I want to ask you to do.
Not because an algorithm needs engagement.
Not because a page needs another impressive number.
But because conversations like this can help people examine what they have been taught and return to the Scriptures.
Or have you witnessed a church faithfully teaching both generosity and repentance?
You do not have to reveal anything you are uncomfortable sharing. But your experience, expressed truthfully and graciously, may help someone who has been silently struggling.
Not as a public performance.
Not as a requirement for a blessing.
But as a sincere expression of the desire to put Christ back at the center.
And if you have experienced the mercy of Jesus after a season of spiritual confusion, consider sharing your testimony. Someone who has nearly given up may need to hear that restoration is possible.
You may have a relative who is questioning their faith.
A friend who feels guilty because they cannot give.
A pastor who needs encouragement to preach the whole counsel of God.
A struggling believer who needs to be reminded that Jesus has not abandoned them.

We want this to be a place where biblical truth is not sacrificed for popularity, where repentance is never separated from grace, and where Jesus Christ—not wealth, influence, or human personalities—remains the center.
Not to buy God's favor.
Not to fulfill a mandatory tithe.
Not because you will be promised financial blessings in return.
But because you believe Scripture-centered discipleship, Gospel proclamation, spiritual encouragement, and the sharing of Christian resources are worthy of voluntary support.

That support can help us continue producing Christ-centered articles, biblical teaching, devotionals, and discipleship content, and pursue broader outreach to people who need to hear the message of Jesus.

For those who want to glorify God through supporting Gospel ministry, this is one practical opportunity to participate. It is not the only way. Faithful prayer, service, sharing biblical truth, generosity toward people in need, and commitment to a local church also matter deeply.
We would rather see you care responsibly for those entrusted to you than give under pressure.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and Christian learning accessible beyond financial barriers.
These products are optional. They are not spiritual necessities, and purchasing them does not make anyone a better Christian.
Not to build a kingdom around a personality.
Not to turn desperation into revenue.
Not to make Christianity sound like a shortcut to wealth.
But to keep pointing people back to the One who alone can save.
Jesus Christ.
The One who confronted sin without abandoning sinners.
The One who spoke truth without manipulating the wounded.
The One who welcomed the broken without selling them access to mercy.
The One who died for our sins, rose from the grave, and calls us to repent and believe.
Because one day, every earthly account will be left behind.
The titles.
The properties.
The applause.
The platforms.
The wealth.
The things we fought so hard to accumulate.
And when that day comes, the question that matters most will not be how much money we managed to acquire.
It will be whether we belong to Jesus Christ.
So pray for provision.
Work faithfully.
Practice wisdom.
Give generously as you are able.
Support trustworthy ministries with a willing heart.
But never confuse the gifts of God with God Himself.
Never allow a promise of prosperity to replace the preaching of repentance.
And never forget that the greatest miracle is not a sinner becoming wealthy.
It is a sinner being reconciled to God through the blood of Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy is not leaving this world without riches—it is spending your life chasing God's blessings while missing the Savior who offered you Himself.
